title: What is the standard contingency fee for R&D tax credit advisors?
description: There is no official or regulated standard contingency fee for R&D tax credit advisors serving U.S. businesses.
summary: There is no official or regulated standard contingency fee for R&D tax credit advisors serving U.S. businesses. Advisory firm commentary puts typical percentage-of-credit fees at roughly 20% to 40%, most often cited as 25% to 40%. Federal rules under Circular 230 and the reportable-transaction regulations may limit these fees or trigger Form 8886 disclosure.

body.text: There is no official or regulated standard contingency fee for R&D tax credit advisors serving U.S. businesses. Advisory firm commentary puts typical percentage-of-credit fees at roughly 20% to 40%, most often cited as 25% to 40%. Federal rules under Circular 230 and the reportable-transaction regulations may limit these fees or trigger Form 8886 disclosure.
It is general information, not legal or tax advice.
Short answer

There is no official or regulated "standard" contingency fee for R&D tax credit advisors. No statute, Treasury regulation, or IRS publication sets a market rate for R&D credit engagements, and the IRS does not publish fee surveys for this service. The figures in circulation come from advisory firms describing the market:

items: Source Advisors states that contingent percentages generally range from 25% to 40% of the amount recovered.
Froehling Anderson states that boutique R&D firms typically charge 35% of the credits generated.
TaxCredit.ai describes specialist-firm fees of 20% to 30% of the credit.

body.text: Read together, these commentary sources put typical percentage-of-credit fees between roughly 20% and 40%, with the 25% to 40% range coming from a single firm. Each source is a provider describing competitors' pricing, and several promote an alternative fee model, so the figures are market commentary, not measured data.

Whether such a fee is permitted, and what it triggers, depends on federal rules covered below: Circular 230 §10.27 (and the court decision limiting it), the December 2024 proposed amendments to Circular 230 that would replace §10.27 (still not finalized as of the verification date), and the reportable-transaction rules for "contractual protection."
How a contingency fee is defined

Circular 230 defines a contingent fee at 31 CFR §10.27(c)(1) as a fee based wholly or partly on whether a return position avoids IRS challenge or is sustained by the IRS or in litigation. The definition expressly includes a fee calculated as a percentage of the refund reported on a return or of the taxes saved, and it also reaches arrangements in which the practitioner reimburses the client (for example, through an indemnity or guarantee) if a position is challenged or not sustained. The rule applies to fee arrangements entered into after March 26, 2008 (§10.27(d)).

A percentage-of-credit R&D fee fits this definition: the fee rises and falls with the credit claimed. The December 2024 proposed regulations (REG-116610-20) would carry a substantially similar definition into a new §10.51(b)(2), covering fees based on a percentage of the refund or taxes saved, fees dependent on specific tax outcomes, and arrangements with reimbursement if a position is contested. A percentage-of-credit R&D fee would therefore remain a "contingent fee" under either the current text or the proposed text.
What the market figures mean in dollars
The credit the fee is taken from

The research credit is in IRC §41. Qualified research expenses (QREs) under §41(b) are in-house research expenses (wages for qualified services, supplies, and certain computer-use payments) plus contract research expenses, which count at 65% of the amount paid to non-employees (75% for qualified research consortiums).

Under the Alternative Simplified Credit in §41(c)(4), the credit is 14% of QREs exceeding 50% of the average QREs of the three preceding taxable years. If the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of those three years, the credit is 6% of current-year QREs.

ADP describes the credit as typically 6% to 8% of annual eligible costs. This is a commentary estimate, not a statutory rate; the statutory rates are the 20% regular credit and the 14% (or 6%) ASC rate applied to the incremental computations described above. Unused general business credits carry back one year and forward 20 years under IRC §39(a)(1).
Fee as a share of the research budget
Hypothetical, recomputed:

items: Fee as a share of QREs: $2.40 ÷ $100 = 2.4%.

body.text: At the low end of ADP's range, the same 30% fee on a 6% credit consumes $100 × 0.06 × 0.30 = $1.80, or 1.8% of QREs. TaxCredit.ai makes a related point, defining net benefit as the credit retained after all fees, and noting that a 20% to 30% fee leaves roughly $70,000 to $80,000 of a $100,000 credit.

Budget predictability
Source Advisors notes that a contingency fee is less predictable for budgeting because the final fee depends on the amount recovered, while a fixed fee is agreed in advance regardless of time spent.
Is a contingency fee allowed? Circular 230 §10.27
The rule as written

Section 10.27(b) prohibits practitioners (attorneys, CPAs, enrolled agents, and others subject to Circular 230) from charging a contingent fee for services in connection with any matter before the IRS, with four exceptions:

items: services connected with the IRS's examination of, or challenge to, an original return;
services connected with an amended return or refund claim filed within 120 days after the taxpayer receives written notice of an examination of, or challenge to, the original return;
a refund claim filed solely in connection with statutory interest or penalties assessed by the IRS;
any judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code.

body.text: Correction: the prohibition is narrower in practice

In Ridgely v. Lew, No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC), 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), Judge Christopher R. Cooper held that the IRS lacked statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. §330 to regulate the preparation and filing of "Ordinary Refund Claims" (refund claims filed after the original return but before an IRS audit begins), and permanently enjoined enforcement of §10.27's contingent-fee restrictions for those claims. Accounting Today reported that the IRS did not appeal, so the decision is final. The text of §10.27 has not been amended and still appears unchanged in the eCFR.
Hierarchy of authority: a final court judgment limiting a regulation outweighs both the regulation's unamended text and practitioner commentary. The result:

items: Original returns: a contingent fee for preparing an original return claiming the R&D credit remains within §10.27's prohibition, which Ridgely did not address.

Amended returns and refund claims filed before an audit: Ridgely bars the IRS from enforcing §10.27 against contingent fees for preparing and filing these claims. Many R&D credits are claimed this way, which helps explain why percentage fees persist in the market.
Advisors outside Circular 230: CohnReznick notes that consultants who are not CPAs, attorneys, or enrolled agents operate under different rules and may price as a share of savings.

body.text: Update: proposed Circular 230 amendments (REG-116610-20)

On December 20, 2024, Treasury and the IRS released proposed regulations (REG-116610-20), published in the Federal Register on December 26, 2024, to update Circular 230. Responding to Ridgely, the proposal would remove §10.27 entirely, withdraw the never-finalized 2009 contingent-fee proposal, and instead classify certain contingent fee arrangements as "disreputable conduct" under a new §10.51(b). Under that proposed section, charging a contingent fee in connection with the preparation of an original or amended tax return, or a claim for refund or credit prepared before examination of the return, would be disreputable conduct subject to sanction; charging an unconscionable fee would also be disreputable conduct.

Treasury's stated rationale is that, while Ridgely limited the IRS's ability to regulate ordinary refund claims as "practice," Treasury retains authority under 31 U.S.C. §330(c) to sanction practitioners for disreputable conduct. Professional bodies, including the AICPA, the ABA Section of Taxation, and the New York State Bar Association Tax Section, filed comments opposing per se treatment of contingent fees as disreputable.

Status: no final rule adopting REG-116610-20 was identified as of November 10, 2026, and current §10.27 remains in the eCFR. Proposed regulations are not binding. For R&D credit engagements, the practical consequence is that the Ridgely-based room for contingent fees on amended-return and pre-audit refund claims could narrow for Circular 230 practitioners if the proposal is finalized in its proposed form, and any legal challenge to a final rule would be decided on its own terms. Taxpayers and advisors negotiating multi-year percentage-fee agreements should watch for a final rule and its applicability date (proposed to be 30 days after publication of final regulations).
The "capped fee" structure

Baker Tilly's commentary describes providers who avoid the prohibition by capping their fee based on calculated or anticipated credits rather than credits actually received. It states that the hourly rates under this structure are generally high compared with other providers, and that no part of the fee is refunded if the IRS later disallows the credit. These are one firm's characterizations of competitors; no IRS guidance addressing capped R&D fees was found.
Conflict on audit support

Froehling Anderson states the opposite for boutique firms: audit defense is built into the contingent fee, although the firm's cost-to-benefit ratio worsens if an audit reduces the credit. Practice varies by engagement letter; neither claim describes the market as a whole.
Contingency fees and reportable transactions

Under Treas. Reg. §1.6011-4(b)(4), a transaction has "contractual protection" if the taxpayer has a right to a full or partial refund of fees when the intended tax consequences are not sustained, or if fees are contingent on the taxpayer realizing tax benefits. The rule covers only fees paid to a person who makes or provides a statement about the transaction's potential tax consequences. A taxpayer who participates in a reportable transaction must attach Form 8886, Reportable Transaction Disclosure Statement, to each relevant return and send a copy to the Office of Tax Shelter Analysis (OTSA) on first filing (§1.6011-4(a), (d), (e)).

Rev. Proc. 2007-20, §4.02 (effective January 26, 2007) excludes fees related to eight credits from the contractual-protection test, including the work opportunity credit (§51) and the low-income housing credit (§42(a)). The research credit under §41 is not on the list, as CohnReznick observes. A percentage-of-credit R&D fee can therefore fall within the contractual-protection category. The regulation also has an exception (§1.6011-4(b)(4)(iii)(B)) for advice given only after the taxpayer has entered the transaction and reported it on a filed return, where no earlier fees were received; whether it applies depends on the facts.
Correction: penalty range for failing to file Form 8886
Under §6707A(b), the penalty is 75% of the decrease in tax shown on the return as a result of the transaction, subject to these limits:

cells: Maximum, reportable transaction that is not listed

body.text: Contractual protection is a non-listed category, so for an R&D engagement whose only reportable feature is a contingent fee, the range is $5,000 to $50,000 (with the $5,000 floor and $10,000 ceiling applying to natural persons, and the $10,000 floor and $50,000 ceiling applying to other taxpayers). The $200,000 ceiling applies only to listed transactions.
Audit exposure behind the fee

Aprio states that claiming the credit on a timely filed return does not automatically trigger an audit, and that an unsuccessful examination can lead to full disallowance and additional penalties. Where a contingency fee is non-refundable, the taxpayer bears the full fee even if the credit is lost.

That expectation is dated. Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration report 2026-IE-R003 (issued March 25, 2026) states that, as of January 2026, Congress had cut IRA funding to $26 billion through rescissions totaling $53.5 billion, $41.8 billion of it from enforcement, leaving $3.8 billion for enforcement. A later TIGTA report (2026-3S0-045, issued August 26, 2026) states that the IRS exhausted that remaining $3.8 billion of IRA enforcement funding as of December 31, 2025, and projects fiscal year 2026 enforcement spending about 29% below fiscal year 2025.

Under the Form 6765 instructions (Rev. December 2025, released in final form in February 2026) and IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025. Reporting remains optional for qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit, and for taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less who claim the credit on an original return. Separately, research credit refund claims postmarked after June 18, 2024, must identify each business component and its research activities and report total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses; the IRS has extended the 45-day perfection period for such claims through January 10, 2027. Because many contingent-fee engagements are built around amended-return refund claims, these documentation requirements directly affect the work an advisor must perform to earn a percentage fee.
Analysis: does "no benefit, no fee" avoid the contingency rules?

As analysis only: §10.27(c)(1) covers fees based "in whole or in part" on whether a position is sustained, and §1.6011-4(b)(4)(i) covers fees contingent on realizing tax benefits. A fee that is waived when no benefit results is at least partly contingent on the outcome. The proposed §10.51(b)(2) definition in REG-116610-20 would use similarly broad outcome-based language. Whether a given engagement letter falls within any of these rules depends on its terms; taxpayers should obtain advice on their specific arrangement.
Conclusion

The most-cited "standard" contingency fee for R&D tax credit work is 25% to 40% of the credit (Source Advisors), with other providers citing 35% for boutiques and 20% to 30% for specialists. These are commentary figures, not regulated rates. On a credit of 6% to 8% of QREs, a 30% fee absorbs about 1.8% to 2.4% of the research budget (0.06 × 0.30 = 1.8%; 0.08 × 0.30 = 2.4%). Circular 230 §10.27 still bars contingent fees for original-return preparation, but Ridgely v. Lew removed the IRS's ability to enforce it against ordinary pre-audit refund claims. Proposed regulations (REG-116610-20) would replace §10.27 with a rule treating contingent fees for preparing original or amended returns and pre-examination refund claims as disreputable conduct; they had not been finalized as of November 10, 2026. Because the research credit is not excluded by Rev. Proc. 2007-20, a contingent R&D fee may make the engagement a reportable transaction requiring Form 8886, with a §6707A penalty of $5,000 to $50,000 for failing to disclose a non-listed transaction.
